blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we are recording at 2513 Dan Neal, Mr. Ernest Rubelow. How do you pronounce your name?
Rubelow.
Rubelow.
Rubelow.
How's that spelled?
R-O-U-B-L-E-A-U.
L-E-U. And the date is the 18th of October 1961. This is Bill Russell doing the interviewing. Do you mind telling just where you were born and when you were born, your birthday, when it is?
I was born in 1896. 1896. In St. Charles Parish. St. Charles, is that up the river? It's about 40 miles from here. What was the exact birthday? When is your birthday?
December the 26th. The 26th, the day after Christmas?
That's right.
Can you tell us what you remember of your mother and father? You mentioned your father was a musician you told me a minute ago.
Well, I remember that my father...
Y'all want to see this card on the card if I get?
That's all right. That's all right. I remember my father was in a brass band. He played the brass band. What was his instrument? His instrument was a B-flat trumpet.
B-flat trumpet. What was his name, his first name?
Charlie Rublo. Charles. Mm-hmm.
Did they have a brass band in St. Charles?
They had a brass band at that time.
Well. Was it like the bands here? Did they sound a good deal like as far as you can remember?
It's been a long time since they had been. Absolutely. Absolutely. That was real music. Absolutely sound.
About how big a band was it?
Do you remember? They had 15 pieces. Really? A little bigger than the years now. Yeah, that's right. 15 pieces. Brass band.
Mm-hmm. Did they have many parades there?
Well, now and then it had parades in our hometown.
Did they ever play for dances? Did they have any dance music? Did the brass band play for dances by any chance?
Well, not as I remember.
Yeah. Do you remember what kind of dance bands they had?
Well, I do remember you used to have four and five pieces of dance band. Did your father play in any of those? Was he playing?
Yeah. Oh, yes. He was playing.
For dances, too. He was playing. Mm-hmm.
Did they sound much different than the small jazz bands they have here now? Or how did the music sound in those days, if you can remember? What kind of music you heard?
Well, the kind of music that I heard was the same Dixieland music that they're playing now. And other words, they had some very good musicians in that band.
Did any musicians from New Orleans ever come up there that you heard?
Well, now there's musicians from New Orleans used to come out into my hometown to play, too. What is the name of the town? Was it the... Colonna, Louisiana.
Colonna. Oh. What other larger town is that? Is it near Baton Rouge up that way? No. Or Lafayette or how? What's the direction? I don't know.
No, that's about nine miles from Lulon. Lulon. Lulon.
It's up the river there.
Mm-hmm. On the other side. On the other side.
I remember. I was over there once.
Huh?
Anything else about your family? Did anyone else, your mother play anything?
My mother couldn't play her anything. But my mother could sing very good, but all French.
Yeah. Did she sing in any churches or any religious sacred music?
Well, she sung songs and she sang sacred music, too. But my mother sung mostly all French's numbers, French songs. Yeah. In other words, she couldn't speak 15 words in English.
French, very French. I knew it's a French name that you have. That's right. Were you raised to speak French when you were a boy?
Well, I did. I learned it mostly about her. Of course, my daddy could speak it, too. But not as pure French as my mother could speak French.
I wondered if you heard any church music in those days. Were you all... Did you belong to the Catholic Church or any other church?

Well, we all belonged to the Catholic. I've been to the Catholic. I'm still Catholic now. And they had a benevolent association. It's a society that used to play for the parade. The society is here. The society is over there. They used to play parade just like those people parading here.
I wondered, did they ever have music with the funerals like they have here, the brass band?
Not as I remember that.
You don't remember the funerals? No. That brass band, did they ever jazz up any of the numbers? You know, like here they get swinging pretty much out on the street like they do in the dance.

Pretty good jazz, I'll tell you. Thank you, with the brass band, too. That's right. They had some trumpet players in there with my father. It was under the flag. I've heard a man who's trumpet player here. Of course, this man is dead now. Yes. He got drowned. His name was De Jong. Now, what his last name was, I don't know. His name was De Jong.
Same name like Harold De Jong?
Same name, but I don't know his first name, but his name was De Jong.
And he was a trumpet player.
De Jong was about the sweetest trumpet player that anybody wanted. He wanted to hear. Otherwise, De Jong was something like Buddy Bowling. Of course, I don't know Buddy Bowling.
Everybody talks about him. He must have been very great. Very, very great.
Something clear.
That's right. Anybody else in your family? Do you have any that played music? Any brothers or sisters or uncles?
Well, I had a brother that played banjo and guitar. The part of his dad now. Is he older than you? I'm older than him.
Oh, you were older than him. I wonder just when you took up music, how old you were?
When I took it up, I was 15 years old. My first instrument was the violin.
What violin? I play violin too. Yes. Yes. Did you have lessons? Your father helped you with that? Or how did you learn that?

My father helped me with the violin because he told me one day, he says, why don't you try to learn how to play some music? So I said to him, I says, I don't believe I'm going to learn that. So he said, yeah, try. I believe you can learn it. Well, I used to watch him playing his violin. After he'd go to work, and I know where he saved the violin right on top of the almo. You know, it was all the time. He put it up there, and I told my mother. I told my mother, I said, I said, Mama, I said, get the violin down and let me play something. My mother gets it down and give it to me. And I go into the room and come in and saw it around, saw it around on it for about a couple of months. I beat him playing the violin. Then he gave it to me. I just gave up the violin for about 16 years.
Yeah, I didn't know you ever played that one.
That's the first instrument.
Your first instrument.

All right. From the violin. What, did you play in any bands or orchestras with that? At that time? Yes. The violin. I and my brother, that stayed, used to play for parties over in Luling, two pieces, violin and guitar.
Yeah, I've heard of the small groups like that.
Violin. We used to play violin and guitar. Just I and my brother.
Yeah.

Well, after I put the violin down, I came right after the war. I was here in 1919. I've been here ever since. You moved here right after the war. Right after the war. When I got demobilized out of the army, I came here and lived here. I've been here ever since. All right. I bought a band jewel in 1920 from Grunewald Music Store. Yeah. Not Grunewald. Where are lines? C.G. Conn.
Oh, Conn. Yeah. They had a story.
I bought a tenor van jewel. It cost $150 there. And learned that the first band that I started playing with when I bought the van jewel, it was Jack Carrey's band.
Oh, yeah. I knew his brother Mutt, but I never knew Jack Carrey.
Well, Mutt, I know Mutt, too. Well, I started playing with Jack. I played with Jack a very long time. Then, jumps around and played with Chris Kelly.
Can you tell us who else was in the band when you played with Jack Carrey?
But, Jack, as far as I can remember, I can call some of the names.
Yes.
You mean you want the name?
Yes. Any of the other people, the other instruments. How big a band was it? Do you remember about how many?
How big the band was? No more than six pieces. Six. Six pieces. Well, Jack Carrey and the same fellow that going trumpet now, Punch. Oh, Punch, yeah. He was going trumpet.
He told me he played his own.
And Joseph Phillip was a bass violin player.
Oh.
Joseph Phillip.
Was that the same, wait a minute? Babe, they called him Babe. Called him Babe.
Babe, yeah, that's it. He died.
I knew him.
He was our bass player.
I'm making some records with him one time.
He was our bass player. Babe. And Jack Carrey. And myself. And Punch. Let's see who they had on drums. Well, he did have a regular drum player. Sometimes he'd grab, uh... Goodness.
Let me call this drum player.
Yeah. Sometimes he'd grab a little fella named Voynell Joseph.
Oh, I've heard of him.
I don't know. I never did know. Well, sometimes he'd grab him on his drums.
Remember who the clarinet player was?
Yeah, no. The clarinet player, and I... Let's see. Sometime he'd have... This fella, Burybank. Sometime he'd have Burybank with him. Play clarinet.
Punch said he used to play some of the Georgia Boy. Georgia Boy. Did you see in the band?
Georgia Boy? Yeah. Sometime he'd have Georgia Boy. Sometime he'd have Georgia Boy with him.
Where did you all play in those days?
In those days?
What kind of jobs did they have?
Where did we play in those days? Different parts. Morgan City. Uh... Lake Charles. Morganser. St. Jones Parish. Several around. In my parish in Kelowna. And, uh... Mandeville, Covington. Oh, yeah.
All around.
Oh, yeah. Mandeville, Covington. And, uh... Slidell. Yeah. Bugaloosa.
Mm-hmm.
Biloxi. Paschristine.
Yeah. Oh, yeah. I didn't know they traveled so much.
Oh, yeah.
You were playing banjo with them then?
Playing banjo then.
You started on the banjo then before guitar.
I first started on the violin then... Yes, I mean... And then after the banjo, it was guitar.
Then you took up the guitar later.

That's right. Did you have any teachers on those other instruments? I had to teach on the banjo, but not on guitar. Who helped? My father helped me with the violin. Yes. But I had to teach it on the banjo from, uh... This man, Dave Perkins, who died.
Dave Perkins. I've heard of him. I never knew him.
He lived right there on 6th Street between Dryden and Verona.
I've heard of him.
Dave Perkins was a nice fellow, though. He's teaching white and black.
Yes. They say he was very light.
I think he looked like he was white, they tell me. He couldn't hardly tell it.
What was his main instrument? Do you remember?
Oh, Dave.
Did he ever... Yes. Dave Perkins. Did he ever play in banjo?
What was his main instrument? Well, I don't know. He played everything. He played everything, huh?
That's right.
Was he working in any band in those days? Oh, Dave Perkins?
Yes, or was he just teaching?
Dave Perkins was teaching in all those parades at that time. He was playing in the white bands in the parade.
That's right.
Do you remember what method you had or any books or anything?

No, I don't remember the methods that Dave Perkins had. That's the one they started teaching me from. I don't remember the methods. But I don't think it's very much different than the methods they have now.
Probably about the same thing.
The same thing.
40 years ago, but I guess not much different. Can you tell us, after you left Jack Carey and you say you went with Chris Kelly?
After I left with Jack Carey and played with Chris Kelly a while. Played with him a while and then jumped around and played with Rene a couple of times.
I heard Ted Rene, but I never heard Chris Kelly either.
Chris Kelly was.
I never heard Jack Carey. Can you tell us more about Chris's band, who else was in it? What kind of music they used and all.
And Chris Kelly, they were using the same thing as those people are using today. Clarinet, trumpet. Of course, Chris, he played the trumpet.
Phil, I knew you.
And I think Chester was playing bass for Chris. Chester's artist.
I knew him.

He was playing bass for Chris. And Chris, let's see who he had on clarinet. Sometimes he had Georgia Boy with him, you know. Different fellas he'd had with him on clarinet. And... And... Now, the fellas that he had in his heart, if... I can't memorize those fellas.
It's hard to remember all the different names. Is it about the same size band as Jack Carey?
Jack Carey, sometimes he would have six, sometimes seven. See, well, at that time, a seven-piece band was really a National Dixie Land band.
Yeah.
Of course, today, they may cut it down to six, but they leave the main instrument out. It's the band, you know, they leave that out.
Yeah, the band's now leaving out.

Yeah, leave that out. So, for instance, over there. Yeah. Now, why I was over there? Because the bass player was sick or he couldn't show up. Well, I was over there. Yeah. But, in my time, if a band couldn't get a band's old player, he'd have to dig up.

one somewhere they're gonna get a banjo regardless they're gonna have ten pianos Did they use piano in those days much? They used piano in those days when they had them use them but they would never cut the banjo. Yeah keep that first. That's right never cut the banjo off. Yeah. See in other words there's lots of places that we
has played and didn't have a piano one. I've seen a lot of places too that way.
I have no piano in it. No piano at all. Oh that time it was a seven piece Dixieland man it was a seven piece. That's right. Yeah.
When did you get your guitar? Did you switch over then from banjo to guitar?

Well I switched from banjo to guitar. I got the guitar in 1943. I got the guitar in 1943. A lot later than you started on banjo. Oh banjo was after I left the violin I jumped on the banjo. Yeah. Yeah that was around 1919. Jumped on the banjo. Yeah right after the war. That's right.

Yeah. Did you like the guitar or the banjo best? Well I like the guitar. Of course I like the banjo too but other words the guitar play much easier than the banjo. It seems easier. It is to me it is rather easy. Those extra strings to me it seems like it would be a little harder maybe with six strings than the four. I play violin I only had four strings. That's right. Six strings would bother me. Did you have any lessons on the guitar or just picked it up yourself? On the guitar? Well I Did you have any lessons on the guitar or just picked it up yourself?
On the guitar? Well I got me a self-instructor book and got some ideas from that and I kind of learned the guitar some.
Yeah.
Now I have a steel guitar here. I had to take lesson one. I got a self-instructor book on that. Like what you call the Hawaiian guitar? That's right.
I never did know how they were playing.
That's a sweet music. That steel bar they slide along. That's right. It's steel right in front of me. Yeah.
But you just worked it out yourself and learned the fingering and all.
I worked it out myself with the steel. Some beautiful numbers on the Hawaiian guitars. Yeah.

You might tell us about some more of the bands you played with like you mentioned. Some more about Chris Kelly's band. Where did they play? Do you remember some of them? Where did they play? Any special jobs that you can remember that they had?
Well they played over at the, they used to have a Bulls Club here.
Oh yeah. That's right down here.

On 8th Street. Played many times at that Bulls Club. Different bands played there many times. We played there. Played there several times with Jack and Chris Kelly and uh, and Rene at the Bulls. All right. And we used to go in Biloxi, Mississippi, and Peakyune, Mississippi, and Magnolia, Mississippi, McComb, Mississippi, all in there. Can you tell us anything about Chris Kelly's style? How he played? What he sounded like? I mean... Chris Kelly stuff playing now, the same thing. And I had some very good ideas about the Dixieland music, and there's lots of Dixieland numbers that I really knows. And they had some very good musicians at that time. Very good.
Remember, some people told us that Chris was real good on the blues. Do you remember any of the blues numbers that he played?

Well, you know why they said Chris was very good on the blues? Chris was the first trumpet player that when they put out the Chalice Love, he took a toilet flush and made a wah-wah with that in his trumpet and everybody went wild. Not only the blues and the thing he played it was that.
He used that all the time.
No, he used it all right, but he naturally could play some trumpet. Oh, yeah. Don't you forget that. He could play some trumpet.
What style did he have? Did he play loud or soft mostly? High notes or low or soft? Oh, yeah.
Sure, he'd reach high notes. Absolutely. Good range and all.
I don't know if he just stuck down on the staff or...
No, well, when he'd go above the staff, he'd go. When he didn't have to go, he just didn't go. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Any other jobs that you all had in town here? Any certain clubs, some of the old halls you used to play at? Do you remember?
Yeah, we played over at the... used to have a hall on the South Street called the Saint-Sue.
See, they tore that down, I guess, later.

Yeah. I never looked up inside. Oh, that place was in a bloom. The Saint-Sue, the Corporate Hall downtown, the Frantz Amis, all of that. Yeah. Chris had that sewed up. And when Chris wasn't there, Jack had it sewed up. That's right.
He played a lot of those old halls there.
That's right. He played lots of... lots of Dixieland stuff there. I'm telling you, yes, it did.
Those mostly dances or...
Lots of it.
Bonkays or what all did you have?
Oh, well, eh... It wasn't no... says no rock and roll, no jitterbug dancing, nothing like that. Real dancing. Yeah. And very nice dancing. Like that.
Yeah, better than good.
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that music was naturally... On to the fact that there's no difference to my idea and hearing it and the time that we were playing way back.
Yeah. I was going to ask about Buddy Petit. Buddy.
Played with Buddy Petit.
Yeah.
We played with Buddy Petit a solid two weeks in Mandeville.
Oh, over there.
Now, Buddy had Mandeville and Bugalooza sewed up.
Some people told me he lived over there for a while. Do you remember him? That's correct.
Yeah, he did. He did live there.
I never got to hear him either.
I had forgot him since you brought him up.
Yeah.
And you were with him in two weeks straight in Mandeville. No. You're talking about the sweet trumpet player that was that. Buddy Petit.
Everybody says he was great. I never got to hear him now.
Great trumpet player. That's right. Yeah. He was a great little trumpet player, Buddy Petit world.
Do you remember the place you played? What kind of a certain dance hall or club or something?
Well, I had a dancing hall over in Mandeville. Dancing hall over in Bugalooza.
You had a regular dance hall there.
And we played a couple times at the hotel in Mandeville.
Yeah.
That was the year around 1921. 21 to 22.
Yeah. Remember who else was in Buddy Petit's band?
Well, I could remember a few, I think.
I see.
Buddy Petit, myself, Earl Foster. And Buddy had a clarinet player that lived over there, too. His name was Fritz.

Oh, yeah. There was in the door Fritz that George Lewis talked about. Now, you're talking about a clarinet player. Oh, my goodness. You think George Lewis was good, isn't it? George says he was wonderful. He's great. I say you think George Lewis is good, huh? Sounds good to me.
He sounds good to you. But if you had to hurt Fritz.
Really great, huh? Sorry I missed him.
My goodness. I don't know if the man's still living.
No, I'm pretty sure he's dead. I never did. George Lewis said he was dead. I'm sure he must have known him.

When I went to Mandeville to play with Buddy, and Fritz came up on the bandstand, we tuned up and everything, and we'll start the playing, and that man played more clarinet than any man that I ever heard. Really? Never heard. That's right.
I think George Lewis says that, too. He said he's the greatest...
I'm not kidding, and I knows when a man can do something.
He said he never came over on this side of the lake. Never did. He doesn't play over here,
so nobody knows him who's over here. Never did.
You got to hear him play with him. I wish I could have heard that.
I could always play with that man.
I wish I hadn't heard that. God dolly.
I played up some banjo during that time that I was really playing up some banjo. Of course, I've been off a banjo for a long time, trying to get back.
I know it's hard. If you don't play all the time, it's a little rough, but it sounds good to me, though. But, uh...
I played up some banjo at that time.
Is there anything about Prince that you can tell us anything about his style? Did he get around real fast, or a big tone, or high notes? Low register. What did he do? Low register. Low register.
High register. Just any way you want it.
It's everything he needs to do.
That man would make monkey jump out of clarinet.
He's really good. I'll work right now.
That's right.
I wish I hadn't heard him.
And I would love for you to year into it. Yeah, sure. At that time.
Never made any records, and nobody much knows anything about him anymore today. No.
Well, at that time, the people wasn't very hot at so much record like that.
No, that's right. They didn't even make them.
Oh, they want that jazz music. That's his. Yeah. In other words, they didn't have very much autophonic, or nothing like that at that time.
Oh. Oh. That's what they want. Oh, Dad, Mom.
I'm not going to play with you today.
Go put your shoes on. Come over here. Go put your shoes on. Look at him. Well, the kids want to see what's going on. Don't worry about it. Oh, really?
Mm-hmm.
Good kid.

I'm going to finish telling you about Fritz. Oh, yes. Fritz was a man. If we had a break in his song, and Fritz didn't hardly ever was familiar with the song, we'd tell him, so watch out, Fritz, you've got a break, and Fritz's going to come out with a sweeter break than what we made. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Fritz was something like Bechet. Of course, I don't know Bechet.
This fellow that died. I knew he was in New York, is all I knew he might have. I don't know him. Eight years.
But I've heard his records, but I don't know him. Never saw him. Otherwise, Fritz and Bechet played enough clarinet for me.
Because he's natural players, I guess. Natural talent for him. That's right.
And the boys would shoot up some clarinet.
Do you know if he had anybody else in his family that played the instruments, or how he might have learned, or anything about it?
I didn't know none of his family.
You never did talk about how he learned,
or how he got started in music? No. Well, we never did probably had that kind of conversation.
Yeah, on the job, you don't get much time to talk sometimes.
And in other words, we didn't see him all that much until we get a job to play.
Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
That was with Buddy Petit's band.
Yeah. That was with Buddy Petit. Buddy Petit was living in Mandeville then at that time. Buddy had Mandeville sort of, he had all Mandeville, all Bogaloosa, and Slidell.
How did Buddy sound compared to, say, Chris Kelly? Did they, anything in life, or different?
Yeah, oh yeah, it had to be different, it's different in the trumpet sounds, mostly any trumpet. That's right, yeah,
I know people play quite a lot, but I'm just wondering, there's any special differences in their style?

In my judgment, Buddy was faster on his finger than Chris Kelly, but Chris Kelly had a stronger tone in his trumpet than Buddy. Yeah. but all the same number that Buddy were playing, Chris was playing him the same thing. He was playing him. Mm-hmm. such as Panama Rag, and, and, uh, tailgate ramblers, all of that stuff, you know?
that type of number.
Oh yeah.
And you say you played something with Kid Rene, too?
That's right.
How was he? Who else was in his band? Do you remember who else played with you? Well,
he had, uh, on bass, I think he had, sometime he had Chester, sometime he had a fella called Simon, you know?
Well, them around already, Simon,
uh-huh. And, uh, sometime he had Mealy Bond, different fellas, you know, that I can remember. Yeah. Yeah.
How did he sound compared to Chris and Buddy Petty? Was he?
Who?
Uh, uh, Kid Rene, was he much different style?
Different style? No, it was no different style in the playing. It was no different style in the playing at all. It was the same Dixieland jazz. Yeah.
Same Dixieland style that they have today. That's right. It's still sound modern today.
The same thing they have today, the Dixieland style today, the same thing.
Yeah. Do you remember who was his drummer or some people
who was, who was, who was the drummer at that time?
Or, Kid Rene.
Oh, Rene?
Yeah.
No, he had some fella downtown and it could, it could have been Saeed, it could have been somebody else but I don't remember that.
Yeah, I think his brother played with him sometimes, I think. His brother is right down here on Jackson, you know, the church, Jehovah's Witness church. Yeah, yeah. Joe Rene. Joe.
Joe Rene.
Can't think what kid Rene is. Henry was his name, wasn't it? Henry.
That's right. That's right. That's the brother of a witness.
Remember who his clarinet player was?

Who, a buddy? No, kid Rene. No, Rene? Well, sometime Rene would have... This fellow. Sometime he'd have Burbank. When he couldn't get Burbank, sometime he'd have a Georgia boy. And his regular clarinet player just came to me now. His name was Zeb.
Oh, Zeb. That's what I've heard of him. I never did know him.
Zeb. Zeb Le Norris.
Zeb Le Norris.
Uh-huh. That's his name. Zeb Le Norris. How did he sound? Who, Zeb? Zeb naturally adakes the line clarinet player. Yeah.
Yeah.
Oh, yeah. That was a standby clarinet player.
That's right. That's right. This tape is up about over. I got another reel. There's only a half hour on each reel here.
By the time it gets straight, I get a cigarette.
Yeah, go ahead. You got... I got a little scissors here. I don't see if I can cut that off. In those days, you were always playing the banjo then?
At that time. Yeah. That's what I was on, the banjo at that time.
Did anybody much play guitar in those days in the banjo?
I didn't see any.
Everybody was...
Banjo.
When you got your guitar, where did you get that? Was it by that run the music stores here too?
You can ask anything you want to do.
Did you like the guitar as well as the banjo for a small Dixieland band, as they call them now, the Dixieland band? Or did you...
Small Dix...
Did you like banjo better than guitar? Which one is the best, do you think, part of it?
Well, I want to thank I likes the guitar better myself.
Why do you like it better? Is there any special reason?
Well, it is a reason. It plays much easier to me.
Just playing easier, huh?
Mm-hmm.
I can't find my pencil. Keep on talking. And you didn't have a teacher on the guitar. Just pick that up.
Just pick that up. Yeah. Mm-hmm. What do you want, a pencil?

I have it. I have it. There's some place out there. I'll get you. Let's be my other... There's a little pen. I'll find it. It'll be in one of my pockets. It's going to write on the box, you know. There it is.
Right here.

Oh, yeah. Here. I have one before. Thanks. Some people think the guitar isn't loud enough for a band nowadays that they can hear the banjo easier. Could you play the guitar loud enough without the electric amplifier to make it hurt in the band?

Well, the guitars that they have now, they're made especially for the amplifier that you cannot hear them in the band now. So, the banjo, you can hear them in the band. Banjo is kind of imitating a drum.
Yeah, it has that drum head on it. Mm-hmm. That's right. After you took up the guitar, do you remember which bands you played with? That was in the 30s, was it?
After I took up the guitar? Mm-hmm. After I took up the guitar, well, I played with different outfits. Oh, yeah. Just small outfits, you know. Nothing much to talk about.
Was there any especially famous bands or musicians you played with after you left? Chris Kelly and Kid René and those people?
No, in the morning, I played with Kit Thomas for about two or three years.
I didn't know you were in that long, right?
With Kit Thomas.
Is that across the river, most of them?
With Speck and Long Road.
With Specks and all?
That's right.
I used to go to Specks.
I was playing guitar there. Yeah. We had 11 pieces there during wartime.
Well, a big band there.
Big place. Yeah, that's right. Needs a big band.
Yeah, that's right. Any other bands around that time that you might have worked with?
Well, you mean after Kit Thomas?
Well, yes, or even before that we might have missed.
After Kit Thomas, well, I joined in with Foster Lewis' band. Foster Lewis.
Foster Lewis, yes.
Yeah.
I've heard of him but don't know him.
Now you're talking about a trombone player. That's a sweet trombone player. Very sweet.

Speaking of banjo and guitar players, who were your favorites of the other musicians in the old days when you were starting out? Who did you like to listen to? Did you listen to some of the others when you weren't working? Did you ever go to here?
Did I listen to the other bands?
Yes. And which banjo players did you like?
Did I like to be your best? Yes. Which were the best players? Well, I will tell you. I had a little cousin. He was playing with P. Ron on the roof garden.
Oh, yeah.

segments.title: Recording set-up and birth in St. Charles Parish
segments.summary: Russell announces the recording location and date and has Roubleau spell his name; Roubleau says he was born December 26, 1896 in St. Charles Parish.

segments.title: Father's brass band in Colonna
segments.summary: His father Charlie played B-flat trumpet in a 15-piece brass band and in small dance bands in the hometown of Colonna; New Orleans musicians sometimes came to play there.

segments.title: Mother's French songs and the Catholic church
segments.summary: His mother could not play but sang French songs and sacred music and spoke almost no English; the family was Catholic and the society had a band for parades.

segments.title: Jazzing up the brass band and trumpeter De Jong
segments.summary: No funeral music he remembers, but the brass band played pretty good jazz; he praises a drowned hometown trumpeter named De Jong as very sweet, like Buddy Bolden.

segments.chapter: Early music and the Jack Carey band
segments.title: Brother and learning violin from his father
segments.summary: His younger brother played banjo and guitar; at fifteen Roubleau taught himself violin on his father's instrument and played parties in Luling with his brother.

segments.chapter: Early music and the Jack Carey band
segments.title: Moving to New Orleans in 1919 and joining Jack Carey
segments.summary: After demobilization he settled in New Orleans in 1919, bought an instrument from C.G. Conn in 1920 and first played with Jack Carey, then Chris Kelly.

segments.chapter: Early music and the Jack Carey band
segments.title: Jack Carey's band: personnel and towns played
segments.summary: Names the six-piece band: Carey and Punch on trumpet, Babe Joseph Phillip on bass, drummer Voynell Joseph at times, and clarinetists Burbank and Georgia Boy.

segments.title: Banjo, guitar and learning from Dave Perkins
segments.summary: He played banjo in those bands and later took up guitar; his banjo teacher was Dave Perkins, a light-skinned man who taught white and black pupils and played in white parade bands.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
segments.title: Chris Kelly's band and why the banjo was never cut
segments.summary: After Carey he played with Chris Kelly and a few times with Kid Rene; Kelly's band had clarinet, trumpet and Chester on bass, and a seven-piece band was standard, always with banjo.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
segments.title: Switching from banjo to guitar and the steel guitar
segments.summary: He got his guitar in 1943, prefers it because it is easier, learned it from a self-instructor book, and likewise taught himself steel guitar.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
segments.title: Chris Kelly's jobs at the Bulls Club and in Mississippi
segments.summary: Kelly, Carey and Rene bands played the Bulls Club on 8th Street and towns in Mississippi such as Biloxi and McComb.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
segments.title: Chris Kelly's trumpet style and plunger effects
segments.summary: Kelly was known for blues and a wah-wah effect using a toilet plunger in his trumpet, but could also play high notes and had a good range.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
segments.title: Dance halls like the San Su and what the dancing was like
segments.summary: Halls such as the San Su on South Street were dominated by Kelly and Carey; the dances were real dancing, with no rock and roll.

segments.title: Playing two weeks with Buddy Petit in Mandeville
segments.summary: He played a solid two weeks with Petit, who lived in Mandeville and had Mandeville, Bogalusa and Slidell sewed up, at a dance hall and the hotel.

segments.title: Fritz, the great clarinetist in Petit's band
segments.summary: Roubleau lists Petit's band with Earl Foster and clarinetist Fritz, whom he rates above everyone, compared to Bechet; Fritz never recorded or played across the lake.

segments.title: Buddy Petit compared with Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Petit was faster on the valves while Kelly had a stronger tone; they played the same numbers such as Panama Rag and Tailgate Ramblers.

segments.title: Kid Rene's band and its clarinetists
segments.summary: He played with Kid Rene, whose bassists included Chester and Simon, whose style was the same Dixieland, and whose regular clarinetist was Zeb Le Norris.

segments.title: Tape change
segments.summary: Russell notes the reel is nearly over and a new one is needed.

segments.title: Banjo versus guitar in the band
segments.summary: Banjo was the only instrument then; he prefers guitar because it is easier, was self-taught on it, and says modern guitars need amplifiers while the banjo carries in a band.

segments.title: Guitar years with Kid Thomas at Speck's and Foster Lewis
segments.summary: After taking up guitar he played small outfits, then two or three years with Kid Thomas at Speck's, an eleven-piece band during wartime.

segments.title: Caffrey Darensbourg, the banjoist at the roof garden
segments.summary: His favorite banjo player was his younger cousin Caffrey Darensbourg, a fast lead player at the roof garden who learned mandolin in their hometown first.

segments.title: The Darensbourg family and Willie Foster
segments.summary: Russell asks about Joe Darensbourg and Willie Foster; Roubleau says Caffrey's family came from his hometown, his father played mandolin and guitar, and Caffrey died in Texas.

segments.title: Surviving members of his father's band and uncles
segments.summary: None of the old hometown band is alive; only one of nine uncles survives and only his father played music.

segments.title: Small outfits during the Depression and the WPA band
segments.summary: He was not in the WPA band but played small outfits on guitar when the banjo was out, with young players who knew nothing of Dixieland.

segments.title: Other banjo players: John Marrero
segments.summary: He recalls John Marrero, who played with Papa Celestin, and Russell talks about the Marrero brothers.

segments.title: Favorite bands to hear and six nights a week at the San Su
segments.summary: When not working he heard Piron's band with his cousin; he describes six nights in succession at the San Su and Jack Carey's band being heard everywhere.

segments.title: Tiger Rag and the trumpeters who filled in for Carey
segments.summary: Carey's band played Tiger Rag with no special arrangement; Punch, Buddy Petit or blacksmith-trumpeter Peter Lacalle filled in on trumpet.

segments.title: Manuel Perez as a favorite trumpeter
segments.summary: Roubleau calls Manuel Perez an excellent, sweet trumpet player.

segments.title: Playing at the Cottage Inn
segments.summary: He played a four-piece at the Cottage Inn near St. Louis Street with a pianist, Harold Dejan on saxophone and himself on banjo.

segments.title: Buck Jones, a trumpeter he admired
segments.summary: He liked hearing Buck Jones, who played with Jack Carey several times before going north.

segments.title: Favorite guitarists after the banjo went out
segments.summary: After banjo faded he liked Johnny St. Cyr best, also Homer Eugene and Narvin Kimball, who started on guitar in Papa Celestin's band.

segments.title: Early music: little blues, marches and mother's opera
segments.summary: As a boy he heard marches and songs from the brass band but little blues; his mother sang mostly opera and French songs.

segments.title: Giving up music in the Depression and buying a guitar in the war
segments.summary: He sold his instrument in the Depression, bought a guitar in 1942 or 1943 and has played it since with Kid Thomas and others.

segments.title: Parents' deaths and living in the neighborhood
segments.summary: His father died in 1939 at 81 and his mother at 78, both in the same neighborhood where Roubleau settled after World War I.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Russell thanks Roubleau and ends the interview.
